conceptTag: Why printers are cheap and ink is not
readerTitle: Why the printer costs less than its ink
caseNote: 실제 관찰 (프린터 업계의 가격 구조, 잉크 탱크 프린터) + 가상 사례 (사무용품 매장, 카페 결제 단말기) · 수치는 모두 설명용
insight: 싼 본체와 비싼 소모품 모델은 잠금이 유지될 때만 돈이 된다. 그래서 고객을 묶는 장치보다 고객이 머물 이유가 더 오래 간다.
misconception: 본체를 싸게 팔고 소모품으로 벌면 언제나 남는 장사다. 고객을 기술적으로 묶어 두면 이익이 안전하다.

sources.text: 프린터 업계의 일반적 가격 구조(본체 저마진, 잉크 고마진)에 대한 업계 보도와 관찰
잉크 탱크(리필 병) 방식 프린터 제품군에 대한 제조사 공개 자료
모든 가격과 비용 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 3번 카드 계산(가상 수치, 유통 마진 등은 단순화를 위해 생략): 본체 $60 − 제조·배송 $70 = −$10. 잉크 3년간 6세트 × $40 = $240, 잉크 제조 원가 합계 $40 → 잉크 이익 $200. 합계 −$10 + $200 = $190.
5번 카드: 일부 제조사가 카트리지 칩과 펌웨어 업데이트로 타사 카트리지를 거부해 소송과 일부 국가 규제 당국의 제재를 받은 사례가 있다는 일반적 서술입니다. 특정 회사·금액·연도는 쓰지 않았습니다. 게시 전 대표 사례를 확인하세요.
6번 카드: 본체를 더 비싸게 받고 잉크를 병으로 싸게 파는 잉크 탱크 프린터가 여러 제조사에서 판매된다는 내용을 확인하세요. 잉크 정기구독 서비스가 존재한다는 일반 서술도 확인 필요.

cards.title: Why the printer costs less than its ink
body: You need a printer. The store has a decent one for $59. Next to it hangs a replacement set of ink cartridges for $45.
Two refills and you've paid more for ink than for the machine. Nobody in this aisle made a mistake. The price tags are doing exactly what they were designed to do.

image.label: A cheap printer next to an almost equally priced ink pack on a store shelf
image.brief: 전자제품 매장 선반. 왼쪽에 "$59" 가격표가 붙은 프린터, 오른쪽에 "$45" 가격표의 잉크 카트리지 묶음. 두 가격표 크기가 거의 같아 보이게. 실제 브랜드 로고와 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You run an office-supply store.
body: A supplier offers a popular printer that leaves you only a few dollars of profit per unit. Its cartridges fit no other printer, and they leave you a healthy margin.

options.text: Stock the printer at a thin margin and keep its cartridges always in stock
options.feedback: This is **razors and blades** from the shelf side: the printer brings the customer, the cartridges bring them back. It only works if you never run out of refills.

options.text: Skip it. A product that barely earns isn't worth the shelf space
options.feedback: You judge the printer alone and miss years of cartridge sales that follow it. A rival store gets those return visits instead.

options.text: Raise the printer price to earn a proper margin on it
options.feedback: You earn more per printer but sell fewer, since shoppers compare that price everywhere. Fewer printers sold means fewer customers who need your refills later.

cards.title: Follow one printer for three years.
body: Simplified, with made-up numbers. The sale everyone sees loses money. The sales nobody notices pay for everything.

breakdown.detail: Sold for $60, costs $70 to make and ship

cards.title: Razors and blades
body: You met this model earlier: price the base item low, then earn on the refills it needs. The printer is the razor. The ink is the blade.
It works under two conditions. The refills must be bought again and again, and they must be tied to the base. A printer that used any ink would turn the $10 loss into a plain loss.
cards.callout: The model is a bet that the customer comes back for refills, and buys them from you.

cards.title: Lock-in keeps the blades yours.
body: Cheap compatible cartridges exist. So makers work to make switching awkward: special cartridge shapes, chips that the printer checks, warnings about warranties.

Some makers have pushed updates that made printers reject other brands' cartridges. That drew lawsuits and, in some countries, penalties from regulators. This is **lock-in** at work: the higher the cost of leaving, the safer the ink margin.

image.label: A cartridge with a small chip being checked by a printer
image.brief: 잉크 카트리지 단면 일러스트. 카트리지의 작은 칩과 프린터 내부를 연결하는 점선, 정품 카트리지는 초록 체크, 다른 카트리지는 빨간 X. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Some printers do the opposite.
body: Several makers also sell ink tank printers. The machine costs much more, and you refill it from cheap bottles of ink.

This turns the model around: earn on the base, not the refills. It appeals to people who print a lot and have done the math on cartridges. Ink subscriptions are another variation, closer to paying per page printed.

image.label: Two printers side by side: cheap with costly cartridges, pricey with cheap ink bottles
image.brief: 좌우 비교 일러스트. 왼쪽: 작은 가격표의 프린터 + 큰 가격표의 카트리지 더미. 오른쪽: 큰 가격표의 프린터 + 작은 가격표의 잉크 병. 실제 상표 없음.

cards.title: Lock-in that feels like a trap backfires.
body: The cheap base is a loan to the customer, repaid through refills. If the lock-in breaks, through compatible refills, new rules or a rival model, the loan is never repaid.
Forced lock-in also costs trust. Customers who feel trapped stay only until they can leave, then warn others. Lock-in from convenience and quality lasts longer than lock-in from chips.

cards.title: Now it's software for cafés.
body: You sell a checkout app for cafés. It runs on a tablet and card reader. You earn a small fee on every card payment.
How do you price the hardware?

options.text: Give the hardware away, lock it to your payments only, and set a high fee
options.feedback: Classic **razors and blades** with hard **lock-in**. It works until a rival offers the same free tablet with lower fees, then resentful cafés leave as soon as they can.

options.text: Sell the hardware near cost, keep fees fair, and make menus, reports and staff training live in your app
options.feedback: A low base still brings cafés in, and the fees are the blades. The **lock-in** comes from how much work your app saves, so customers stay because they want to.

options.text: Charge full price for the hardware and offer the lowest fees
options.feedback: Safer cash today, with no loss to recover. But a big upfront bill slows sign-ups, and small cafés often can't afford it.

cards.title: A cheap base only pays if customers keep buying the refills from you.
body: **Concepts used:** razors and blades (earn on refills, not the base) and lock-in (what keeps those refills yours). The best lock-in is a reason to stay, not a wall.
**Try it today:** find one thing you sell that customers buy again. Ask what keeps them buying it from you: habit, quality, convenience, or only the hassle of leaving?
